note: Curated, human-reviewed facts. Every entry names the source it was checked against, gives a `source_url` a reviewer can open, the `checked_on` date somebody last held the claim against it, and a `claim_type` from the closed vocabulary in `nba_peak/nba_facts/validation.py`. The build refuses any entry with `verified: false`, an empty `source_detail`, missing claim metadata, or language a source cannot settle.

facts.headline: Basketball invented the shot clock because one game finished 19–18.
facts.body: On 22 November 1950 the Fort Wayne Pistons held the ball for minutes at a time and beat the Minneapolis Lakers 19–18, still the lowest-scoring game in league history. Four years later the NBA adopted a 24-second clock, and scoring jumped 13.6 points a game in a single season.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com and Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame accounts of the 24-second clock's adoption; Time, 'How the Shot Clock Saved Basketball'

facts.headline: The 24-second clock is not a round number. It is division.
facts.body: Danny Biasone, who owned the Syracuse Nationals, took the 2,880 seconds in a game and divided by the 120 shots two teams were then averaging between them. The answer was 24, and the professional game has used it ever since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame profile of Danny Biasone; NBA.com and Time, 'How the Shot Clock Saved Basketball'. NOTE: the Hall of Fame and Le Moyne College's NBA-in-Central-New-York archive co-credit Nationals general manager Leo Ferris with the calculation.

facts.headline: Nobody filmed the 100-point game.
facts.body: Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 in Hershey, Pennsylvania on 2 March 1962 as Philadelphia beat New York 169–147. No television cameras were there. What survives is a fourth-quarter radio recording a college student, Jim Trelease, made off a late-night rebroadcast using a radiator as an aerial — now held by the Library of Congress.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Library of Congress National Recording Preservation Board, 'Fourth quarter radio coverage of Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point game'; NBA.com top moments, 1962

facts.headline: The Dream Team exists because of a vote the United States lost.
facts.body: In Munich in April 1989, FIBA voted 56–13 to let professionals into the Olympics. The American federation was among the thirteen against. Three years later the Dream Team walked into Barcelona.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com and Britannica accounts of FIBA's April 1989 Munich vote and the 1992 Barcelona tournament

facts.headline: The Dream Team's first Olympic opponent was Angola.
facts.body: On 26 July 1992 in Barcelona the first team of NBA professionals to play at an Olympics beat Angola 116–48. It was the United States' opening game of the tournament, and the margin was 68 points.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com and Britannica accounts of FIBA's April 1989 Munich vote and the 1992 Barcelona tournament

facts.headline: The NBA adopted the three-point line as a one-year experiment.
facts.body: It came in for 1979–80, three years after the league inherited the shot from the ABA and declined to use it. Chris Ford of the Celtics made the first one on 12 October 1979 against Houston.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Doubt, disdain marked most NBA teams' first forays into 3-point land'; CBS Sports on the 1994-97 shortened line

facts.headline: For three seasons the NBA moved the three-point line in, and it backfired.
facts.body: From 1994–95 the arc was a uniform 22 feet, 21 inches closer at the top. Attempts rose by more than half — and scoring kept falling. The line went back where it was after 1996–97 and has not moved since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Doubt, disdain marked most NBA teams' first forays into 3-point land'; CBS Sports on the 1994-97 shortened line

facts.headline: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's first NBA game was a 29-point double-double.
facts.body: 18 October 1969, for Milwaukee against Detroit: 29 points and 12 rebounds, at 22 years old. He would go on to hold the league's career scoring record for thirty-eight years.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 'This Week in History: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's NBA Debut'; Basketball-Reference game log, 18 October 1969

facts.headline: One record stood for thirty-eight years and fell on a turnaround jumper.
facts.body: On 7 February 2023, with 10.9 seconds left in the third quarter, LeBron James hit a 21-footer for his 38,388th point and passed Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. Abdul-Jabbar had held the record since April 1984.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com scoring tracker and NPR/CNN reports of 7 February 2023

facts.headline: The only Latin American team ever to win Olympic basketball gold did it by beating the United States.
facts.body: Argentina knocked the Americans out 89–81 in the 2004 semi-final, Manu Ginóbili scoring 29, then beat Italy for gold. Since men's basketball entered the Games in 1936, no other side from the region has won it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com, 'We broke the spell, the aura of the invincible USA'; ESPN on Argentina's 2004 gold

facts.headline: The WNBA's first game was played in the Lakers' arena, two years before the Lakers left it.
facts.body: The New York Liberty beat the Los Angeles Sparks 67–57 at the Great Western Forum on 21 June 1997. Eight teams started: Charlotte, Cleveland, Houston, Los Angeles, New York, Phoenix, Sacramento and Utah.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com history timeline; ESPN, 'Inside the WNBA's inaugural game, 25 seasons later'

facts.headline: The WNBA's first signed player gave birth four days into its first season.
facts.body: Sheryl Swoopes was announced on 23 October 1996, before the league had played a game. Her son was born on 25 June 1997, four days after the opener; she made her debut six weeks later, on 7 August, and won the first four championships with Houston.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com history timeline; ESPN, 'Inside the WNBA's inaugural game, 25 seasons later'

facts.headline: Diana Taurasi retired holding the WNBA's career records for points and three-pointers.
facts.body: Twenty seasons, three championships and six Olympic golds. She finished with 10,646 points and 1,447 three-pointers. Tina Charles passed her for career field goals made in September 2025.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: CBS Sports on Tina Charles passing Diana Taurasi for career field goals made, September 2025; WNBA.com career leaders

facts.headline: WNBA attendance rose by nearly half in a single season.
facts.body: The league averaged 9,807 a game in 2024, up from 6,615 the year before, and 2.35 million fans came through the gates — a 48% rise. A Fever–Mystics game at Capital One Arena drew 20,711, a regular-season record that stood until July 2026.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: ESPN, 'WNBA touts 48% attendance jump, 2.3M fans attend games'; Associated Press on the Dallas–Toronto crowd of 20,966 in July 2026

facts.headline: Basketball was invented in two weeks, with a soccer ball and two peach baskets.
facts.body: James Naismith, a Canadian teaching in Springfield, Massachusetts, was given a fortnight to devise an indoor winter game. He wrote thirteen rules and nailed the baskets to the gymnasium balcony — which is why the rim is ten feet up.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Springfield College, 'Where Basketball was Invented'; Smithsonian Magazine and National Geographic accounts of 1891

facts.headline: Real Madrid has won the European club championship eleven times, more than any other club.
facts.body: CSKA Moscow is next with eight. Panathinaikos won a seventh in 2024, thirteen years after its sixth, by beating Real Madrid 95–80 in the final in Berlin.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia's EuroLeague all-time title table, sourced to EuroLeague Basketball: Real Madrid 11, CSKA Moscow 8, Panathinaikos 7; EuroLeague coverage of the 2024 Final Four in Berlin

facts.headline: Australia's national league is older than the NBA's three-point line.
facts.body: The NBL played its first season in 1979, the same year the NBA first tried the three-pointer, and now runs with ten teams — nine Australian and one from New Zealand.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBL Australia official site and league records

facts.headline: Yao Ming played eight NBA seasons and then ran Chinese basketball for seven years.
facts.body: He came from the Shanghai Sharks, went first overall to Houston in 2002, missed the whole of 2009-10 after foot surgery and retired in 2011. He was elected chairman of the Chinese Basketball Association in February 2017 and resigned in October 2024.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference career record for Yao Ming; ESPN on his 2011 retirement and Reuters on his October 2024 resignation as CBA chairman

facts.headline: Portland used the second pick of the 1984 draft on a centre, a year after drafting Clyde Drexler.
facts.body: Sam Bowie went second and Michael Jordan went third to Chicago. Bowie was a seven-foot centre from Kentucky; the Blazers had taken Drexler, a shooting guard, 14th overall in 1983.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Britannica, 'Who was drafted ahead of Michael Jordan?'; 1984 NBA draft records

facts.headline: Only one player from the 1999 NBA draft is in the Hall of Fame, and he was picked 57th.
facts.body: San Antonio took Manu Ginóbili with the second-to-last pick of the second round. He did not arrive in the NBA for another three years.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference draft record, 1999; Pounding The Rock on the 1999 class's only Hall of Famer. NOTE: expires before the 2027 Hall of Fame class is announced, because the claim is a standing rather than a result.

facts.headline: Nikola Jokić was drafted 41st, and the pick was announced during a commercial break.
facts.body: Denver took him in the second round in 2014, thirty-eight places after Joel Embiid. He was playing for Mega Vizura in Serbia, and most NBA teams had seen him only at that April's Nike Hoop Summit in Portland.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA Draft and Denver Nuggets records, 2014 second round; ESPN, 'Why was Finals MVP Nikola Jokic the 41st pick?'

facts.headline: The longest winning streak in major American professional sport is 33 games, and it is more than fifty years old.
facts.body: The 1971–72 Lakers won every game from 5 November to 7 January. Milwaukee, with Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Oscar Robertson, beat them on 9 January.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Lakers, 'The '72 Lakers' 33-Game Win Streak'; NBA.com on the Bucks ending it

facts.headline: The man who ended the Lakers' 33-game streak spent most of his career winning titles for them.
facts.body: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's Bucks stopped the run on 9 January 1972. He was traded to Los Angeles in 1975 and won five championships across fourteen seasons in the uniform he had beaten.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Lakers, 'The '72 Lakers' 33-Game Win Streak'; NBA.com on the Bucks ending it — cross-referenced with Abdul-Jabbar's career record on Basketball-Reference

facts.headline: Willis Reed played Game 7 of the 1970 Finals on a torn thigh muscle and scored four points.
facts.body: He tore it in Game 5, missed Game 6, and walked out of the tunnel for Game 7. He made the Knicks' first two baskets and did not score again. New York won 113–99.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com top Finals moments, 1970 Game 7; Naismith Hall of Fame biography of Willis Reed

facts.headline: The Flu Game was Game 5, not Game 6, and it was not the closer.
facts.body: Michael Jordan scored 38 against Utah on 11 June 1997 while barely able to stand, and hit a three with 25 seconds left for the lead. Chicago won 90–88, and the series still needed another game.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com top Finals moments, 'Michael Jordan flu game', 1997 Game 5

facts.headline: Miami's tying three in Game 6 of the 2013 Finals came off an offensive rebound.
facts.body: The Heat trailed 95–92 with seconds left. LeBron James missed; Chris Bosh took the rebound and kicked it out; Ray Allen backpedalled into the right corner and tied it with 5.2 seconds on the clock. Miami won 103–100 in overtime and took the series in seven.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com top Finals moments, 'Ray Allen 3-pointer, Game 6, 2013 Finals'

facts.headline: Robert Horry has more championship rings than Michael Jordan, and was never an All-Star.
facts.body: Seven, with three different franchises: two in Houston, three in Los Angeles, two in San Antonio. He averaged 7.0 points a game across sixteen seasons.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference career record; San Antonio Sports Hall of Fame biography

facts.headline: One franchise won eight championships in a row. No other has won four.
facts.body: Boston took every title from 1959 to 1966 under Red Auerbach, with Bill Russell at centre for all of them — eleven in thirteen seasons. The longest run by anybody else is three.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Boston Celtics' NBA championships'; Britannica on the 1959-66 run

facts.headline: One rule change added more scoring in a season than the three-point line ever has.
facts.body: NBA teams averaged 79.5 points a game in 1953–54. With the 24-second clock, they averaged 93.1 the following season — a 13.6-point jump from a single rule.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com and Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame accounts of the 24-second clock's adoption; Time, 'How the Shot Clock Saved Basketball'

facts.headline: The NBA spent three years with the three-point line in its possession and refused to use it.
facts.body: The ABA had used the shot since 1967. The leagues merged in 1976, four ABA teams joined, and the line stayed off NBA floors until 1979–80 — adopted then only as a one-year experiment.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Doubt, disdain marked most NBA teams' first forays into 3-point land'; CBS Sports on the 1994-97 shortened line

facts.headline: The first Olympic basketball final was played outdoors, in the rain, and finished 19–8.
facts.body: Berlin, 1936, on converted clay tennis courts. The United States beat Canada in rain that made dribbling close to impossible. Every Olympic five-on-five tournament since has been played indoors.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Olympics.com, 'Olympic basketball's muddy beginnings'; FIBA, 'Olympic Games: Berlin 1936'. NOTE: bounded to five-on-five because Olympic 3x3 was played outdoors at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024.

facts.headline: The last three seconds of the 1972 Olympic final were played three times.
facts.body: Confusion over a timeout and the game clock sent Munich back to the same three seconds twice more. The Soviet Union won 51–50, ending a 63-game American Olympic winning run, and the United States players have refused their silver medals ever since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia and HISTORY accounts of the 1972 Olympic men's basketball final; 'Three Seconds in Munich' (University of Nebraska Press)

facts.headline: Lithuania collected its 1992 Olympic bronze in tie-dye the Grateful Dead had paid for.
facts.body: Newly independent and short of money, the team took a donation from the band and sold licensed tie-dye shirts — a slam-dunking skeleton in Lithuania's yellow, green and red — to fund the trip. They wore them on the podium.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Snopes fact-check, 'Did the Grateful Dead Fund Lithuania's Olympic Basketball Team?'. NOTE: Snopes records that the band was one source of funding rather than the only one, and that the tie-dyes were shirts worn at the medal ceremony, not playing kit.

facts.headline: Lithuania calls basketball its second religion.
facts.body: The saying places it behind Catholicism. A country of under three million has taken three Olympic bronze medals, won the EuroLeague through Žalgiris Kaunas in 1999, and sent a steady line of players to the NBA.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Lithuania Travel, 'The Second Religion of Lithuania'; Global Times, 'In Lithuania, basketball is second only to God'

facts.headline: Portland drafted Arvydas Sabonis in 1986 and did not see him play until 1995.
facts.body: He was 24th overall, behind the Iron Curtain, and by the time he arrived his knees had taken the best of him. He still made an All-Rookie team at 31.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia and Blazer's Edge accounts of the 1986 NBA draft and Arvydas Sabonis's arrival in Portland

facts.headline: Dražen Petrović was a third-round pick who became an All-NBA guard.
facts.body: Portland took him 60th overall in 1986 and he arrived in 1989. In his fourth NBA season, with New Jersey, he made the All-NBA Third Team; he was killed in a car accident in June 1993, aged 28.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: 1986 NBA draft record (third round, 60th overall, Portland); ESPN, 'Drazen Petrovic leaves lasting legacy in NBA'

facts.headline: Oscar Schmidt scored 49,737 points for club and country, and none of them in the NBA.
facts.body: He turned down New Jersey after the 1984 draft rather than give up Brazil's national team, and went on playing into his forties in Brazil, Italy and Spain. His career total stood as basketball's highest until LeBron James passed it in April 2024.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia's list of basketball players with the most career points, sourced to FIBA and league records; NBA.com and Olympics.com profiles of Oscar Schmidt

facts.headline: The NBA's African league tipped off in Kigali, in front of a continent that had waited decades for one.
facts.body: The Basketball Africa League played its first season in Rwanda in May 2021, with twelve clubs from twelve countries — six of them national champions with automatic places, six through FIBA qualifying tournaments. It is the first league the NBA has helped run outside North America.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA Africa press release, 'Basketball Africa League 2021: By the Numbers'; Atlantic Council, 'The Basketball Africa League has arrived'

facts.headline: In the Philippines the basketball court is a piece of civic infrastructure.
facts.body: Barangays — the country's smallest administrative unit — build and maintain courts the way other places build playgrounds, and a single neighbourhood can hold several. Backboards get improvised from whatever is to hand, bingo boards included.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Asia Society, '15 Photos Exploring the Filipino Obsession With Basketball'; National Geographic's 'Pinoy Hoops'

facts.headline: The NBA got rid of one defensive habit and scoring went up by nearly four points a game.
facts.body: Hand-checking — a defender resting a hand on the ball-handler to steer him — was outlawed for 2004-05. Teams averaged 93.4 points the season before and 97.2 the season after.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference league per-game averages for 2003-04 and 2004-05; NBA rule-change records for the 2004-05 hand-checking ban

facts.headline: The NBA banned zone defence for decades, then legalised it and added a rule to stop it working.
facts.body: Zones became legal for 2001-02, and the defensive three-second violation arrived in the same package — a defender may not camp in the paint. One change opened the door; the other kept anyone from standing in it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Defensive three-second violation'; NBA rule-change records for 2001-02

facts.headline: The draft lottery exists because teams were visibly trying to lose.
facts.body: From 1966 the first pick was decided by a coin flip between the worst team in each conference, and the incentive was exactly what it looks like. The first lottery, in 1985, sent Patrick Ewing to New York, and a conspiracy theory about a frozen envelope has outlived every attempt to check it — no evidence has surfaced.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: theScore, '30-year anniversary of conspiracy-laden 1985 NBA Draft Lottery'; Bleacher Report, 'The Frozen Envelope'

facts.headline: Wilt Chamberlain once took 55 rebounds off one basketball game.
facts.body: 24 November 1960, against Bill Russell's Celtics. It is still the record, and the man who set it said afterwards he had never been more tired in his life.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: HISTORY, 'Wilt Chamberlain sets NBA rebounds record'; Basketball-Reference box score, 24 November 1960

facts.headline: The single-game assist record has stood since 1990.
facts.body: Scott Skiles handed out 30 for Orlando against Denver on 30 December 1990, breaking Kevin Porter's 29 from 1978. Nobody has matched it since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'This Day in History: Scott Skiles Records 30 Assists in a Game'

facts.headline: Kobe Bryant scored 81 points in a regular-season game his team won by 18.
facts.body: 22 January 2006, the Lakers beating Toronto 122–104. He took 46 shots and made 28, with seven three-pointers and 18 free throws.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Kobe Bryant's 81-point game', sourced to the NBA box score. NOTE: the entry no longer claims this is the second-highest total of the post-merger era — Bam Adebayo scored 83 for Miami on 10 March 2026.

facts.headline: The tallest and the shortest men in NBA history are separated by two feet and four inches.
facts.body: Manute Bol and Gheorghe Mureșan were both listed at 7 feet 7. Muggsy Bogues was listed at 5 feet 3 and played fourteen seasons. All three were in the league at the same time in 1994-95, though Bol played five games that season before a knee injury ended it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Guinness World Records, 'Tallest NBA player (ever)'; Britannica, 'List of the Tallest NBA Players'; NPR, 'The NBA's shortest player never gave up'; Basketball-Reference listing

facts.headline: Reggie Miller scored eight points in nine seconds, and the Knicks were leading by six when he started.
facts.body: Game 1 of the 1995 Eastern Conference semi-finals at Madison Square Garden: a three, a steal off the inbound, another three, then two free throws. Indiana won 107–105.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Pacers oral history, 'I Almost Fell Over'; Wikipedia, '8 points in 9 seconds'

facts.headline: Tracy McGrady scored thirteen points in the last thirty-five seconds and turned a loss into a win.
facts.body: 9 December 2004, Houston trailing San Antonio 76–68 with 35 seconds left. Four straight three-pointers, one of them a four-point play, the last with 1.7 seconds on the clock. Rockets 81–80.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, '13 points in 35 seconds', sourced to the NBA box score. NOTE: 35 seconds is the game clock when Houston trailed 76-68; NBA.com's video titles the run itself '13 points in 33 seconds'.

facts.headline: The Los Angeles Lakers are named after lakes a thousand miles away.
facts.body: The franchise took the name in Minneapolis, after Minnesota, the Land of 10,000 Lakes. It moved to a city with almost none in 1960 and kept it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Britannica, 'Los Angeles Lakers'; Star Tribune on the Minneapolis-to-Los Angeles move

facts.headline: Utah's team is called the Jazz because it used to be in New Orleans.
facts.body: The name was chosen there in 1974 for its dictionary meaning — collective improvisation — and travelled to Salt Lake City with the franchise in 1979. New Orleans has asked for it back.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Britannica, 'Utah Jazz'; Deseret News and Deadspin accounts of the New Orleans naming and the move

facts.headline: Vancouver's NBA team was almost called the Mounties, until the Mounties objected.
facts.body: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police objected to the name, so the 1995 expansion side became the Grizzlies after the bear native to British Columbia. The franchise moved to Memphis in 2001 and kept it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Vancouver Grizzlies' and 'History of the Memphis Grizzlies'

facts.headline: Toronto's team is named after a dinosaur from a film released the year before.
facts.body: Jurassic Park came out in June 1993, and a fan contest named the expansion franchise the Raptors the following May. It started play in 1995, and the plaza outside its arena is called Jurassic Park to this day.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: EBSCO Research, 'Toronto Raptors'; CBC, 'The birth of the Toronto Raptors (as a logo)'

facts.headline: The NBA's letter was about a different shoe from the one Nike went on to sell.
facts.body: The league's uniform rule required footwear to be mostly white and to match a player's teammates. In February 1985 the NBA wrote to Nike about the red-and-black shoes Michael Jordan had worn the previous October — Air Ships, worn because the Air Jordan 1 was not finished. Nike answered with a television advertisement saying the NBA had thrown the shoes out of the game, and sold the Air Jordan 1 on it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Complex, 'Shipwrecked: The Untold Story Behind Michael Jordan's Banned Sneakers'; Nike, 'How the Air Jordan 1 Banned Colorway Sparked a Sneaker Revolution'. NOTE: the entry no longer says Jordan was fined. Published accounts disagree on whether any fine was levied, and David Stern said afterwards that the shoes were never banned.

facts.headline: The slam dunk contest was invented as a half-time filler by a league about to fold.
facts.body: 27 January 1976, at the ABA All-Star Game in Denver. Five players entered and Julius Erving won it with a dunk from the free-throw line. The ABA merged into the NBA that summer and Erving came with it; the NBA staged its own dunk contest from 1984.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'Slam Dunk Contest'; ESPN Page 2, 'The day the dunk was born'

facts.headline: A 1993 arcade cabinet was the highest-grossing arcade game in America that year.
facts.body: NBA Jam put two players a side, no fouls, and a ball that caught fire after three straight baskets. Midway's cabinet took more money in the United States in 1993 than any other arcade game.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Wikipedia, 'NBA Jam (1993 video game)', sourced to RePlay's 1993 arcade earnings charts; arcade-history.com entry

facts.headline: The Converse All Star is named after a salesman.
facts.body: Converse introduced the shoe as the Non-Skid in 1917 and rebranded it All Star in 1919. Chuck Taylor, a semi-professional player hired to sell it in 1921, did so well that Converse put his signature on the ankle patch in 1932. It has been in production ever since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Nike/Converse, 'The True History of the Chuck Taylor All Star'; Naismith Hall of Fame biography of Chuck Taylor. NOTE: the entry no longer calls it the first basketball shoe — Converse's own account does not claim that, and Spalding sold canvas basketball high-tops around 1900.

facts.headline: One team won the first four championships the WNBA ever held.
facts.body: The Houston Comets took 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2000. The franchise folded in 2008; no WNBA team has won four in a row since.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com championship records; Houston Comets franchise history and the league's 2008 decision to fold it

facts.headline: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is the first player in four years to win back-to-back MVPs.
facts.body: He took 83 of the 100 first-place votes for 2025-26 after averaging 31.1 points on a career-best 55.3% shooting for a 64-18 Oklahoma City team. He is the fourteenth player to repeat, and the first since Nikola Jokić in 2021 and 2022.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2025-26 Kia MVP announcement; ESPN and NBC Sports reports on the full voting ballot

facts.headline: New York won a championship fifty-three years after its last one.
facts.body: The Knicks beat San Antonio 4-1 in the 2026 Finals, closing the series 94-90 in Game 5. Their previous title came in 1973, six years before the NBA had a three-point line.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2026 NBA Finals coverage; ESPN report on Game 5

facts.headline: Jalen Brunson scored 45 points in the game that ended the Finals.
facts.body: All eleven voters gave him the 2026 Finals MVP after he averaged 32.6 points in the series. Only Michael Jordan, Bob Pettit and Giannis Antetokounmpo had scored 45 in a game that closed out a Finals win before him.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Jalen Brunson wins Bill Russell trophy as 2026 NBA Finals MVP'; ESPN Game 5 report

facts.headline: No Defensive Player of the Year had ever been unanimous until 2026.
facts.body: Victor Wembanyama took all 100 first-place votes at 22, the youngest winner the award has had, after leading the NBA in blocks for a third straight season. He arrived from France in 2023 and is the third player, after Michael Jordan and David Robinson, to win both Rookie of the Year and this.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Spurs' Victor Wembanyama named 2025-26 Kia NBA Defensive Player of the Year'; Associated Press and ESPN voting reports. NOTE: 'led the NBA in blocks for a third straight season' follows AP and NBA.com on total blocks (254, 176, 197); ESPN says a second straight, counting only the seasons in which he met the 58-game qualification threshold.

facts.headline: The youngest fifty-point game in NBA history belongs to a rookie.
facts.body: Cooper Flagg scored 51 against Orlando on 3 April 2026, aged 19 years and 103 days. Nobody younger had reached fifty in a league game.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2025-26 Kia Rookie of the Year release; Associated Press report on Flagg's 51-point game

facts.headline: For the first time since Michael Jordan, a rookie led his own team in points, rebounds, assists and steals.
facts.body: Cooper Flagg averaged 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists across 70 starts for Dallas and won Rookie of the Year for 2025-26. Jordan's 1984-85 season was the last time a first-year player topped his team in all four.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: CBS Sports and NBA.com on the 2025-26 Kia NBA Rookie of the Year vote. NOTE: the four-category claim is checkable back to 1973-74, the first season steals were recorded.

facts.headline: The 2026 scoring champion had been traded fourteen months earlier.
facts.body: Luka Dončić averaged 33.5 points a game for the Los Angeles Lakers in 2025-26. Dallas had sent him west in February 2025, in the middle of a season, in a trade that also moved Anthony Davis the other way.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2025-26 season statistics; ESPN reporting on the February 2025 trade

facts.headline: San Antonio won 62 games and reached the Finals for the first time since 2014.
facts.body: The Spurs' 62-20 season was the second-best record in the league in 2025-26. They lost the Finals to New York in five games.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2026 playoff coverage; ESPN 2025-26 standings and season recap

facts.headline: Nobody had played twenty-three NBA seasons before.
facts.body: LeBron James passed Vince Carter's twenty-two in 2025-26, turned 41 during it, and finished the year with 43,440 regular-season points — a scoring record he has held since 2023.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: ESPN 2025-26 milestone tracker; Olympics.com LeBron James career points tracker

facts.headline: A record 135 international players opened an NBA season.
facts.body: The 2025-26 season began with 135 players from 43 countries on opening-night rosters, including a record 71 from Europe. France sent 19 of them and Australia 13.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'NBA rosters feature 135 international players from 43 countries to begin the 2025-26 season'

facts.headline: A'ja Wilson won the WNBA's Most Valuable Player award four times in six seasons.
facts.body: 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, passing Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson, who had three each. In 2025 she also led the league in scoring and won Defensive Player of the Year and Finals MVP — the first player in either league to take all four in one season.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com, 'A'ja Wilson Wins Record Fourth Kia WNBA Most Valuable Player Award'; ESPN and NPR coverage of the 2025 WNBA Finals

facts.headline: Las Vegas swept the 2025 WNBA Finals for a third title in four years.
facts.body: The Aces beat Phoenix 4-0, closing it out 97-86 on the road. A'ja Wilson scored 31 in the last one and made 17 of her 19 free throws.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com 2025 Finals coverage; NPR and Olympics.com reports on the deciding game

facts.headline: A rookie led the WNBA in assists.
facts.body: Caitlin Clark averaged 8.4 a game in 2024, the highest in the league, along with 19.2 points and 5.7 rebounds across 40 starts. She won Rookie of the Year with 66 of the 67 votes.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com 2024 Rookie of the Year release; WNBA official 2024 season statistics

facts.headline: An expansion team reached the WNBA playoffs in its first season.
facts.body: The Golden State Valkyries went 23-21 in 2025 and took the eighth seed — the first expansion side in WNBA history to reach the postseason in its opening year.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: WNBA.com 2025 standings and playoff coverage; Associated Press reports on the Valkyries' inaugural season

facts.headline: Two WNBA players started their own league and built an arena for it.
facts.body: Unrivaled, a three-on-three winter league founded by Napheesa Collier and Breanna Stewart, tipped off on 17 January 2025 in a purpose-built arena in Medley, Florida. Rose BC beat Vinyl BC 62-54 in the first final.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Unrivaled league announcements and Associated Press coverage of the inaugural 2025 season

facts.headline: Germany won a World Cup without losing a game.
facts.body: The 2023 FIBA World Cup finished 8-0 for a German side that beat Serbia 83-77 in the final in Manila. Dennis Schröder was the tournament's most valuable player, and it was Germany's first world title.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball game report, Germany v Serbia, 10 September 2023. NOTE: the entry no longer says Germany had won nothing before — they took EuroBasket in 1993 and again in 2025.

facts.headline: Spain won four European titles and two World Cups in sixteen years.
facts.body: EuroBasket in 2009, 2011, 2015 and 2022, and the World Cup in 2006 and 2019. A Gasol brother played in the first five; by 2022 only Rudy Fernández was left from the 2006 side, and Willy Hernangómez was that tournament's most valuable player.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball tournament archives for EuroBasket and the FIBA World Cup; the EuroBasket 2022 squad list, which contains neither Gasol

facts.headline: Slovenia won EuroBasket without losing a game, with an 18-year-old on the roster.
facts.body: The 2017 team went 9-0 for the country's first European title. Goran Dragić was named the tournament's most valuable player; the teenager beside him was Luka Dončić, who had not yet been drafted.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball EuroBasket 2017 tournament records and final report

facts.headline: A country that no longer exists won five basketball World Cups.
facts.body: Yugoslavia took the title in 1970, 1978 and 1990, and the smaller federation that kept the name won again in 1998 and 2002. FIBA counts all five under Yugoslavia; both states have since dissolved, and the players from the 1990 squad went on to represent several different countries.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball World Cup archives

facts.headline: Only two players have won a EuroLeague title, an NBA championship and an Olympic gold medal.
facts.body: Manu Ginóbili won the EuroLeague with Virtus Bologna in 2001, the NBA title with San Antonio in 2003 and gold with Argentina in 2004. Bill Bradley had done it forty years earlier.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: EuroLeague Basketball and Naismith Hall of Fame biographies of Manu Ginóbili; FIBA records for the 2004 Olympic tournament

facts.headline: Canada's first World Cup medal came in overtime, against the United States.
facts.body: The 2023 bronze-medal game went to overtime and Canada won it 127–118, Dillon Brooks scoring 39 and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander 31. It was the country's first medal at a senior global men's tournament since the 1936 Olympics.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: FIBA.basketball 2023 World Cup bronze-medal game report; Canada Basketball and NBA.com coverage

facts.headline: The first NBA game was played in Canada, and the league was not called the NBA.
facts.body: On 1 November 1946 the New York Knickerbockers beat the Toronto Huskies 68-66 at Maple Leaf Gardens, in front of 7,090 people. The competition was the Basketball Association of America; it took the NBA name three years later.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com's account of the league's first game; The Canadian Encyclopedia entry on the Toronto Huskies

facts.headline: The NBA was created in an office in the Empire State Building.
facts.body: On 3 August 1949 the Basketball Association of America and the National Basketball League met in New York and agreed to merge. The league that resulted had seventeen teams, several of them in towns too small to keep one.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: History.com, 'NBA is born, August 3, 1949'; league records of the BAA-NBL merger

facts.headline: Three Black players entered the NBA in 1950, and which of them was first came down to the schedule.
facts.body: Earl Lloyd's Washington Capitols opened a day before Chuck Cooper's Celtics and three days before Nat Clifton's Knicks, so Lloyd played the first game — 31 October 1950, six points, and a 78–70 defeat at Rochester. Cooper had been the first drafted; Clifton the first to sign a contract.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com, 'Earl Lloyd, Chuck Cooper, Nat Clifton blaze new path in NBA'; Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame biography of Earl Lloyd

facts.headline: The first NBA All-Star Game was proposed by a publicity director and paid for by an owner.
facts.body: Haskell Cohen suggested the exhibition; Celtics owner Walter Brown offered Boston Garden and underwrote the costs. On 2 March 1951, 10,094 people watched the East win 111-94, and Boston's Ed Macauley was named most valuable player.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com history of the 1951 All-Star Game; Guinness World Records entry for the first NBA All-Star Game

facts.headline: The NBA's first Black head coach was also his team's starting centre.
facts.body: Boston made Bill Russell player-coach in April 1966, succeeding Red Auerbach. He won championships in 1968 and 1969 while doing both jobs at once.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: History.com, 'Bill Russell becomes the NBA's first Black coach'; Boston Celtics records of the April 1966 appointment. NOTE: bounded to the NBA — Fritz Pollard co-coached the Akron Pros in 1921.

facts.headline: Bill Russell and Wilt Chamberlain played each other 143 times.
facts.body: Chamberlain outscored him in the large majority of them, 30.0 a game to 14.2; Russell's teams won 86. Russell finished with eleven championships and Chamberlain with two.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference head-to-head records for Bill Russell and Wilt Chamberlain: 94 regular-season meetings (Russell 57-37) and 49 playoff meetings (Russell 29-20)

facts.headline: Four teams survived the ABA, and one that did not made its owners a fortune anyway.
facts.body: The merger of June 1976 took in Denver, Indiana, New York and San Antonio. The Spirits of St. Louis folded, and their owners took a share of the four survivors' television money instead — a deal that kept paying for nearly forty years.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: History.com, 'NBA merges with ABA, June 17, 1976'; Washington Post reporting on the merger and the Spirits of St. Louis settlement

facts.headline: For seventeen drafts an NBA team could simply claim a college player who lived nearby.
facts.body: The territorial pick let a club give up its first-round choice and take anyone from within fifty miles of its arena. It is how Cincinnati got Oscar Robertson and Boston got Tom Heinsohn. It ran from 1949 and was abolished in 1966.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Basketball-Reference NBA draft records, 1949-1965; NBA draft history on the territorial selection rule

facts.headline: A Supreme Court justice, sitting alone, is why players could enter the NBA early.
facts.body: Spencer Haywood signed with Seattle in 1970 while the league still required four years out of high school. On 1 March 1971 Justice William O. Douglas, as circuit justice, reinstated the injunction that let him keep playing; the case settled, and the hardship exception that followed is why later players could be drafted at nineteen.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Haywood v. National Basketball Association, 401 U.S. 1204 (1971) — an in-chambers opinion by Justice Douglas as circuit justice, reinstating the district court's preliminary injunction; NBA and Naismith Hall of Fame accounts of the hardship rule

facts.headline: The NBA waited fifty-five years to say who is in its logo.
facts.body: Alan Siegel drew it in 1969 from a photograph of Jerry West and said so publicly in 2010. The league did not confirm it until 12 June 2024, the day West died, when Adam Silver told the New York Times there had been no doubt about it. West had said he wished they would take him off it.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com Q&A with Alan Siegel; Los Angeles Times 2010 interview and CBS Sports reporting on the logo's origin

facts.headline: The highest-rated basketball game ever played was a college final.
facts.body: Michigan State beat Indiana State 75-64 on 26 March 1979 to a 24.1 television rating, higher than any NBA or college game since. It was the first time Magic Johnson and Larry Bird played against each other.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: Nielsen ratings as reported by Forbes and NCAA.com. NOTE: rating, not audience — by raw viewers, Game 6 of the 1998 NBA Finals drew more.

facts.headline: Boston's parquet floor was made out of scrap wood.
facts.body: Timber was short after the war, so in 1946 the Celtics' court was built from offcuts of red oak: 247 panels bolted together, with dead spots visiting players complained about for decades. It was in use until 1999.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBC Sports Boston and Wood Floor Business accounts of the Boston Garden parquet floor

facts.headline: In 2016 Stephen Curry became the NBA's first unanimous MVP.
facts.body: He took all 131 first-place votes in a season where he made 402 three-pointers — 116 more than the record he had set himself the year before.
facts.source_label: Editorial — checked against a named published source
facts.source_detail: NBA.com 2015-16 MVP announcement; ESPN and Forbes reports on the voting
